utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, ask to have the witness sent into the courtroom, please. (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like first to say good afternoon to the interpreters and to the court stenographers and be sure that everybody can hear me properly, be sure that the booths are working right. Good afternoon to Prosecution and Defence counsel, and good afternoon to General Blaskic. General, have you rested? Do you feel all right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, I have had a rest, and I feel quite well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since you feel good, the Prosecutor can now continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we left off with the 20th of April, 1993 concerning individuals from Gacice who were downtown in the town of Vitez, and just to cover a few things that we left off with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could give the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit 158.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, so the record is perfectly clear, I'd like to give you the opportunity to examine 158 and again to get your bearings on 158, as it is an enlargement of Exhibit 45. So if you could take that exhibit and just compare it to Exhibit 45 so that you're comfortable in stating that the area designated "B" is, in fact, the Workers' University. Because when we spoke last on Friday, you expressed some reservation in that regard. If you could stand up and just take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, let the witness hold that exhibit in his hand so that he's comfortable with that assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, as you can see in the comparison of these photographs, the area designated "A" is, in fact, the Hotel Vitez, whereas "B," some 30 to 40 yards behind it, is, in fact, the Workers' University where the cinema is; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noted for us, General, that -- let me return to the testimony of Brigadier Marin where he said on page 13554, at line 12, and he's talking about the village of Gacice, we can move to line 11: "A The village of Gacice is right next to the town of Vitez, and as far as I know, these civilians were in town, and I cannot say what the exact location was, I cannot say at this point. However, the town of Vitez is not a very big town, so it could have been between the post office, the municipality building, the cinema building, et cetera." Now, is it your testimony, sir, that while your chief of operations and your chief of staff at that time, Brigadier Marin, knew that these civilians were in downtown Gacice, that you did not -- excuse me, that these civilians were in downtown Vitez from Gacice, that you did not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that Brigadier Marin had stayed to replace me when I had gone to Zenica to attend a meeting in the afternoon of the 3rd Corps. I believe that Marin during that period had received some reports from which he could deduce that there were civilians, whereas at that time I was at Zenica at a meeting involved in other activities altogether. I did not receive any information of that kind while I was at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you receive that information after your return from headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I returned late at night, quite possibly some of the reports might have contained information about combat activities in the Gacice area and the status of the civilians in the region, and specifically, I can't quite remember, but I believe that some information contained reports of that kind from the Vitez Brigade commanders or other commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us be clear from your prior testimony, General, you did not leave the Hotel Vitez to go to Zenica until 16.30 on the 20th; isn't that right? Well, after 16.30. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. About 16.30, I left the Vitez Hotel and started out at about 16.30 for Zenica, transported by UNPROFOR vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, did you get information when you returned from the meeting in Zenica that civilians from Gacice had been brought to downtown Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When was that question asked, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's on the top of the screen now. "Well, did you receive that information after your return from headquarters?" It's referring to the exact same content of what Mr. Kehoe put in his question a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then the witness said, "... I can't quite remember, but I believe that some information contained reports of that kind from the Vitez Brigade commanders or other commanders," and I'm following up on that specific information, what information the accused received concerning civilians from Gacice coming to downtown Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what information, General, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, it's almost the same question, a little bit different, but perhaps the witness can give us a very rapid answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you understand my question or would you like me to repeat it, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. What information did you receive when you came back from Zenica about civilians from Gacice being brought to downtown Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving information that civilians from Gacice had been brought to downtown Vitez, but as I said, the possibility did exist, that a report of the Vitez Brigade contained data on combat activities in Gacice and that in that report or in reports of that kind, possibly there was reference to relationships with the civilians. If I were to see any report, this would refresh my memory because I'm talking according to what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on now. The question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me show you Defence Exhibit 364. General, this is a document that you signed on the 24th of April -- in fact, an order that you signed on the 24th of April, 1993, and in the preamble of this order, you refer to the basic principles of international humanitarian law. In this order, you demand in point 1: "1. Respect for and protection of the civilian population affected by the fighting; civilians, by definition, play no active part in these conflicts and therefore cannot be the target of attack." Now, General, I think you told us in direct examination that you had had -- excuse me. I'm receiving a signal from the booth. Okay. General, you told us during direct examination that you had had some training in the Geneva Conventions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean my own personal training when I went through military academy or do you mean training in the HVO that we organised?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about your training in the military academy and training while you were an officer in the JNA. What I'm trying to focus on, General, is your knowledge of the Geneva Conventions in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew, General, that in this period of time, the Geneva Conventions strictly prohibited human shields -- using either civilians or prisoners of war as human shields was a war crime. You knew that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew that the use of human shields was a war crime not only at that time in April of 1993, but I knew that from before, and I never allowed any activities of this kind, nor did I receive any information or reports that there was such conduct from my subordinates. I never received information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me read to you a portion Article 51(7) of Protocol 1 of the Geneva Conventions. This is the 1977 Geneva Protocol 1, Article 51 Subdivision (7), which notes as follows: "The presence or movements of the civilian population or individual civilians shall not be used to render certain points or areas immune from military operations, in particular, in attempts to shield military objectives from attack or to shield favour or impede military operations. The parties to the conflict shall not direct the movement of the civilian population or individual civilians in order to attempt to shield military objectives from attacks or to shield military operations." So, General, you would agree that not only can civilians not be used to protect your troops, civilians cannot be used as shields to protect military facilities? Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I agree with that, and I should like to add that I undertook everything in my power to protect civilians, to enforce the protection of civilians and not to use civilians to protect the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And your question, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, my question to you is: Do you know of anybody in the HVO, in any capacity, that was punished, disciplined, arrested, convicted for using individuals as human shields around the Hotel Vitez on the 20th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never received any information that a live shield was used for the Hotel Vitez, and information of that kind never reached me or my headquarters. So no measures were undertaken as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree, sir, that on the 20th of April, 1993, your chief of operations and your chief of staff was Brigadier Marin, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chief of staff, that is to say, he replaced the chief of staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, during the course of the rest of the war, do you recall any other instance where civilians were brought to downtown Vitez and were placed in the vicinity around the Hotel Vitez? Do you recall any other instance where that occurred?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That they were brought. I don't remember that. I know that throughout that time, in the situation of a civil war, civilians lived in the area together with soldiers, and all the families lived in their own homes along the very front line itself. So this was the same area, ten by six kilometres, where over 70.000 people lived, 35.000 of them refugees, mixed civilians, et cetera. We had no where else to go from that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you would agree, sir, that if civilians or prisoners of war were put in harm's way that would be a war crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Hayman here. The question was asked. I don't think that the witness is denying the contents of the Geneva Conventions. Let's move forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move ahead if we can, General, and I'd like to show you a series of photographs, starting with Prosecutor's 33. The ones that I'm looking for here are the ones that have the designations on it PH203, PH197, and PH198. I think that's 33/6, 33/7, and 33/8. If we could place those on the ELMO. Why don't we just leave that on there, please. That will be 33/8. Thank you very much. Now, General, this is, in fact, the cinema, which is also called the Workers' University, that you noted is 30 to 40 yards behind the Hotel Vitez; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It is 30 to 50 metres away. So it's the cinema and the Workers' University building. It is two buildings combined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that building, sir, contains the headquarters of Mario Cerkez, the commander of the Viteska Brigade; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In the Workers' University section was where Mario Cerkez's headquarters were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you noted for us on Friday that prisoners -- well, you found out that prisoners and civilians had been taken into custody in various locations in the Vitez area, and you found this out on the 16th or the 17th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think it was the 16th. Possibly it was the 17th. I can't remember the date exactly, but I think that possibly it was the 17th, after the return of the negotiators. Those questions were brought up as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, how many prisoners, Bosnian Muslims, did you know on the 17th were in custody in the cinema/Workers' University building?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact data, how many there were. I think the report, that is to say, some documents that I saw at the trial here, by a European Monitor, a figure was mentioned, but I know that there were individuals who came during that street fighting to seek shelter there. Some of them were brought in, others came of their own free will, and others left the cinema building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me read you some of the testimony that has come into evidence, and we will discuss it after I read a few excerpts. General, first I will refer to the testimony of Mr. Sefik Pezer on page 1568, at line 2: "A At 2.00, HVO soldiers entered the staircase of the building, and they fired a burst of fire on the ground. They ran up the steps and said, 'All the Muslims come out.' What else could I do but go out, I and my wife?" Moving down to line 12, this is a quote: "A 'Do not be afraid. There will be no problems, you are just going to the cinema for an interview there and you will be released. Do not panic, do not be afraid.' There were seven or eight Muslims on my entrance. We all headed toward the cinema; my wife was one of the groups. When we reached the cinema they took us into the cellars of the cinema. There were already 20 or 30 people in there, Muslims, of course, who had been arrested, and there were two or three women among them." On page 1569, at line 4: "A I already said that there were 20 or 30 of us, and they kept bringing in more, and that night, that is 16th April, in the evening in the cellar where the boiler room was of the cinema, there were about 70 or maybe even 80 of us. It was too cramped. People could not lie down; we could hardly sit, never mind lie down. All day they kept bringing in people; this was on the 16th, in the afternoon and in the evening." Line 22: "A I went to the cinema hall, and I stayed there until the 30th of April. Conditions were more favourable there than in the cellar." This is now page 1575, line 17: "Q Mr. Pezer, you said previously that you were held in the cinema building until 30th April. Can you tell us about your release, exactly what happened on the 30th and where you went after you were released? A On the 30th April in the afternoon, we heard from the HVO -- from the policemen that there would be some kind of an exchange, and on that day, Sefer Halilovic the army commander came, Sulejman Kalco, and another one, let me remember -- it doesn't matter, maybe I will remember later, on the side of the HVO there was Petkovic, who I did not know, and Mario Cerkez, and apparently they had a meeting." He notes on page 1577, at line 15 that he was released that evening and: "A We went home and the others stayed behind." So this document reflects that he was in custody until the 30th. If we could just briefly touch upon Dr. Mujenznovic's testimony as of the 19th, and this is page 1705, on the 19th, at line 22: "A They asked for me and I went with them to Vitez, to the "Dom Kulture", the cultural centre, we called it the Workers' University, "Radnic Univerzitet", and a cinema hall was there, offices, and headquarters of all the political parties were also in that building." Line 12 on 1706: "A In one office, Mario Cerkez was sitting in that office with Zvonko Cilic, Boro Jozic, Stipo Dzigonjam, Zeljko Rebac, and Zeljko Sajevic. Q Were those people you identified all members of the HVO? A All of them were in uniform with HVO insignia." The next page Cerkez notes -- excuse me, Muhamed Mujezinovic notes the conversation with Cerkez: "A He asked me whether I had heard about Ahmici. I said that I had heard about it. Mario Cerkez repeated that I had to do whatever he ordered me to do. First, he said that the HVO lines in Vitez were broken through, as he said, in the village of Dubravica from the direction of Zabrdje, and that the BH army was advancing, was entering the town towards the chemical factory and was getting into town." On line 15 Cerkez noted that: "A They have 2.223 captured Muslims. He emphasised women, children, and that he would kill all of them." Going on to 1709 at the bottom of the page on line 25 and over to 1710: "A Mario Cerkez said, 'No. You have down here in the basement about 300 people. Choose whomever you want.'" On line 8, Dr. Mujenznovic notes that some of them were pensioners who were sick. Again on page 1711 at line 9: "A There was about 300 people there. I was told that I could choose from among these 300 a group for negotiations." So, General, the testimony indicates that there were approximately 300 prisoners in that building that were kept from the 16th of April until the 30th of April, 1993. Does that square with your recollection, sir, of the events?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I don't remember the exact number. I know the number oscillated. So there were those coming into the cinema during the night and would go home during the day. I know of this kind of occurrence. What I want to emphasise is that I did not allow, permit, or order in any way the detention of Muslim Bosniak civilians in any of the facilities. When I learned that they had been taken into custody, I ordered that humane treatment be exerted and wanted to effect a cease-fire and ensure that security measures, safety measures, and release according to the protocols of the International Red Cross. Because of the security situation and safety situation, I was not able to release them without an insight by the International Red Cross, and I know that the civilian commission, after negotiations in Zenica, had exact records on the number of detainees. I know that they were active under the Chairmanship of the International Red Cross and that the International Red Cross always kept precise records on the number of detainees, the way in which they were released, and the way in which safety and security measures were effected for these civilians to be set free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me read you some testimony from your chief of operations and then chief of staff, Brigadier Marin. This is on page 13447 at line 18: "Q Now, that's the command headquarters of the Vitez brigade, approximately 100 metres from the Hotel Vitez, and on the backside of this building was a connecting building where prisoners were being kept, Bosnian Muslim prisoners; right? A Behind this building, that is to say, on the other side, that is where the cinema should be, and I said that as far as I know, around that building or in that building there were some prisoners, that they were there. Q Now, based on your experience as an officer in the military, a military headquarters is a legitimate military target for the enemy, isn't it? A Yes." So you would agree, would you not, General, that the Viteska Brigade headquarters was, in fact, a legitimate military target for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the building in which the headquarters of the Vitez Brigade was located is a legitimate target, and the building where the prisoners were located is another building, and none of the international representatives of the Red Cross ever asked for the detainees to be dislocated or informed me up until the 30th of April that we were behaving badly with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me read to you a question by Judge Shahabuddeen of Brigadier Marin and his answer on page 13964, line 16. Judge Shahabuddeen asked: "JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN: ... Suppose the enemy wanted to shell Mr. Cerkez; do you, as a military man, estimate that there might have been a risk of a shell either falling on the part of the building occupied by the women or children, or falling hard nearby? A It was possible." So the shelling of the headquarters, sir, given the proximity to the prisoners, could very well put them in harm's way; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that they're two buildings side by side. They could have been in harm's way, but I think that they would have been subject to much greater harm in the town of Vitez, because there was street fighting there in downtown Vitez, and it wasn't safe. As far as I know, from the protocol of the International Red Cross, a precondition for any freeing of the people who had been detained, arrested, was that there should be a cease-fire, that the situation should be safe, and that the protocol of the International Red Cross be respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us deal with an exhibit to just elaborate on your last answer about the safety for these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, this is just simply an enlargement of Exhibit 45 which is on the easel which will make it a little easier to deal with than just dealing with the enlargement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a new Prosecution Exhibit which will be given reference number 47H (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is 45. I think it should be 45H. This is an enlargement of 45.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, 45H. I thought that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I must have heard it incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is, of course, the similar enlargement to that which we discussed previously. Now, the point here that is designated as point A is the Hotel Vitez, your headquarters, point B being the Workers' University and headquarters of the Viteska Brigade, and point C being the PTT building. Now, General, during the course of the 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th, 20th, until the cease-fire, the area depicted in this exhibit was shelled regularly by ABiH forces, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The area was shelled on the 16th and 17th. On the 18th, there was infrequent shelling, very infrequent on the 19th, but the fighting was taking place on the northerly reaches, the approach to the town of Vitez, Krizancevo Selo, Dubravica, from the Zenica direction and from Zabrdze and Pintra. But this particular area from the 18th or 19th onwards was not shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us talk just about some of the testimony that you just discussed with us about not being told by the international community about moving those particular prisoners. Let me show you, while you're looking at this exhibit, if we could also refer to Prosecutor's 529. General, let me read to you paragraph 6, if we can move that up, Mr. Usher, please, paragraph 6 deals with humanitarian -- no, it's on that page. Thank you. It notes as follows in A: "The team visited 62 male Muslim prisoners held in a prison under the HVO brigade headquarters in Vitez. The prisoners were treated well, although they were in a small space for such a large group. The location formally is a violation of the Geneva Convention." With that in mind, General, I would also like you to take a look at a document you received from the Viteska Brigade, Defence 327, which is an operations report from the Viteska Brigade. General, before we look at this particular exhibit, you told us that on the 16th of April, the hotel, the post office, the municipal building, and private homes were shelled. In your testimony, that's at 18513. In this exhibit, Defence 327, you are informed by the Viteska Brigade, about the second paragraph: "Around 1600 hours from the region of Vjetrenica, probably from the road, saddle Vjetrenica-Kuber, Muslim forces shelled the town area of Vitez from a tank (probably a T-34). The municipality building was hit, and the enemy was probably targeting the buildings of the Post Office, the Hotel, Workers' University, as well as the civilian facilities in town." General, moving back, and if we can put 45H back on the ELMO, you knew, General, did you not, that the area of the hotel, designated "A," of the PTT building, designated "C," and the Workers' University, designated "B," were being shelled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already stated that they were shelled on the 16th and 17th. From document 327, we can see that the municipality building was hit, and it states that probably, that is, they assess, that the targets were other facilities as well, but these were not hit. Let me just add that sometime from the 17th or 18th, I ordered that civilians be treated humanely, and you can see that from this report, that there were 62 individuals detained in the cinema. So the number oscillated, and the treatment of those prisoners, according to the assessment of the international representatives, was good. We achieved a cease-fire on the 16th, 17th, 18th, and 20th of April, but the problem was that the BH army did not respect the cease-fire, and it was not possible to have a halt in the hostilities. That would have solved the problem of releasing civilians and all the other questions related to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Preliminarily, General, let me refer you back, and I will refer to this in English, of course, this is Prosecutor's Exhibit 529, and the ECMM monitors note: "The team visited 62 male Muslim prisoners held in a prison under HVO brigade headquarters in Vitez." Now, General, "under the brigade headquarters" means underneath what you describe as the Workers' University; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. They were held in the cinema, as far as I was able to understand, and that is what it said in the report you read out to me, 62 prisoners in the cinema building, not the Workers' University building, but the cinema building. They are two buildings and were always two buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me read this to you again. Mr. Usher, if you could put Prosecutor's 529 on the ELMO, again, the humanitarian section: "The team visited 62 male Muslim prisoners held in a prison under HVO brigade headquarters in Vitez." Now, General, this report reflects that they were, in fact, under Cerkez's headquarters, in the basement under Cerkez's headquarters. Now, General --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that they were in the cinema building. I don't know that they were in the basement. I don't know the layout of the building well. I know that there's a hall downstairs and a big restaurant. So I understand this as being in the cinema building, the 62 that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, isn't it a fact that this building which is connected was a legitimate military target for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think you've already asked that question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, knowing that this building was a legitimate military target and knowing that there were Bosnian Muslim civilians kept under the headquarters, did you order these civilians removed so they were not in harm's way?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Had I had any better solution, that is to say, had I had any safer building, I would quite certainly have issued an assignment like that, to change the accommodation. But the fact that nobody was hit there shows that it was the least bad solution, and it wasn't a bad solution because nobody was harmed, although it was not the best, of course. I talked to a representative of the International Red Cross sometime around the 20th or in between meetings, perhaps it was the 21st, and nobody ever asked me to have the civilians moved. But in a situation, a chaotic situation, with ongoing fighting and general insecurity, I still firmly believed that they were safest there, and some of them even came there of their own free will to take shelter, and others were taken by commanders of the Vitez Brigade. For example, the chief of staff took one of the civilians to his own home, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, General, from your answer that you did not order these civilians removed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had no better option at that time because what I wanted to effect was a cease-fire and general safety and security for the entire region, and that building was one of the safest buildings in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it your testimony that you had no other alternative in all of Vitez, in all of the buildings in Kolonija or anywhere else in Vitez, to put these prisoners except in the basement of the Viteska Brigade headquarters; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think he's answered the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that he's answered. He said what he wanted to tell you. He said that perhaps it wasn't the best solution but it was not necessarily the worst either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, let me ask you this, sir: Did not the Bosnian Croat civilians remain in their apartments, or did you put all the Bosnian Croats in the basement as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that I never ordered, either orally or in writing, anybody to be detained, any civilians to be detained, but I did issue orders on the 16th in the morning, it was around 6.00 in the morning, to sound the general alarm. Vitez was a town that was shelled beforehand by the JNA, and I suppose that the civilians were in the basements and cellars of their own buildings once the sirens had sounded, and that they all expected hostilities to cease, and the creation of safer -- a safer situation for civilians to be set free. So I had no right, apart from the Red Cross, to bring in my own decision and to tell the civilians to go out in the streets. I think that would have been a far worse solution than the solution -- situation in which the civilians found themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me read you my question. If you didn't understand it, I'll repeat it again. Did not the Bosnian Croats remain in their apartments, or did you put all the Bosnian Croats in the basement as well? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that the siren had already sound off and there was general danger. Where they went, I imagine everybody was in the basement. Where was where, that I don't know. Everybody tried to make do. There was general chaos. There was an all-out attack. There were combat operations in 22 different place and this is a very, very insecure situation. At that point in time, I did not have precise information as to whether everybody was in the basement or where they were. There were civilians in Stari Vitez who were protected in a similar way, that is to say, Croats by Muslim Bosniaks, that is to say, members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were civilians in Kruscica who were protected in a similar way, also in Vranjska, also in Vitez, but the situation then was one of general chaos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, the reality of the situation is that it was only Bosnian Muslim civilians who were arrested and put in the basement of this building; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that this went both ways. At that time it was very difficult to see who was detaining who. I think that there is a Prosecution or Defence Exhibit, but I remember it, in relation to private arrests. For example, if a father sees that his son is missing, then he is going to carry out a private arrest. He's going to arrest the first person who comes along so that he could get his son back. The situation was very, very complex, and I focused on that, that is to say, protect civilians who were already detained or who had already been put away, to bring about a cease-fire and create safe conditions so that civilians could be released in accordance with the mandate of the International Red Cross, but the precondition was to have a cease-fire and to stop all combat activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, are you saying that for the reasons which you have given, you cannot tell whether any Croats were held in the cellars?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I already said that I believe that there were Croats in basements, perhaps in the basements of their own buildings or someplace. I already said that there were Croats. Everybody tried to do his best, what they could do. Some of these Muslim Bosniaks came to the cinema on their own because they were afraid and they believed there was safety there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the cinema. There were people held there. Were any Croats held there, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the cinema, I believe that there were no Croats there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you had responsibility for the Bosnian Muslims who were being held captive in the basement of the Workers' University and the cinema; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean? In what sense responsible? As commander of the Operative Zone I was responsible for the entire area, but I already said that I did not issue any orders, nor did I approve, nor did I receive any information to the effect that they would be detained or arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone knew that these Muslims had been arrested and placed in the basement of the cinema and the Workers' University, you, as the commander, could have walked the 30 to 40 yards to that facility or given an order to one of your subordinates to release those people and allow them to go back to their homes; isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not so, and in this way I would have broken a fundamental rule of the International Red Cross, which envisaged that each individual, at least that was our understanding and that's the way it was explained to us, perhaps I didn't understand it properly, that every detained individual had to be reported to the representatives of the International Red Cross, and by abiding to the mandate of the International Red Cross these persons should then be released. There was a person who was intermediating and who was deciding on this mutual release. That is not to say that I had competence over one side to release any detainee or did I ever do that. If there were any kind of detentions or arrests, then we would report all of this to International Red Cross. That is what the practice was on both sides, the HVO and the BH army, in the Operative Zone and in the 3rd Corps. This was during the January conflict as well. I remember when we agreed on the release of civilians. When the International Red Cross representatives disagreed, then we had to stop releasing civilians, because they had said that the situation was not safe enough to have them released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, General, are you saying that you could not release prisoners from a potential military target until they, the civilians, were registered by the Red Cross? Is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The practice and the rule, to the best of my understanding, was that releases had to take place through the intermediation of the International Red Cross. But there's one more thing I wish to mention, not only because of that but also because we did not manage to have a cease-fire, and we did not manage to create a safe environment so that all preliminary actions could be carried out by the International Red Cross and then the detainees could be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when did you find out that the civilians from Ahmici were being held in the Dubravica school? When did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that I do not remember the dates exactly, because I know that sometime around the 20th, from the meeting in Zenica, all authority related to detained persons went to the civilian authorities, that is to say, the civilian commission of the civilian HVO government, that is, and of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina through the International Red Cross. They had all the specific information about civilians. The chairman of this commission for release was working on this. It was Mr. Skopljak on behalf of the HVO, and they were working on the releases and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the area around Dubravica become a front-line position?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the area around Dubravica, a bit to the north of Dubravica, the beginning of the conflict -- well, I'd have to look this up in my chronology when this area was a battlefield. Sometime from the 16th, but if you need a precise date I can look it up in my chronology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sir. Just sometime after the 16th will do. Did you ever issue an order, General, to evacuate those civilians from this front-line position so they wouldn't be in harm's way? I'm talking about evacuating them from the Dubravica school. Did you ever issue such an order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The front line was not in the immediate vicinity of the school in Dubravica, it was a bit to the north. I already said that none of the international intermediaries had asked me to issue an order to relocate the prisoners. Had anybody asked for that I would have done so, but the greatest problem was that we were in such a situation that there was no safe area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, my question to you is this: Did you issue an order to evacuate the civilians from the Dubravica school, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not issue any orders because I had no place to relocate them, and nobody had asked me to do, that. None of the international representatives who were in contact with me had asked me to do that. At that time we were working on a cease-fire and we were working on the creation of safe conditions for the mutual release of civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General when, did the shelling in Vitez stop between the 20th and the 30th of April? What date?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have to look this up in my chronology to see when this happened exactly because the shelling was expressed in different ways. Sometimes the command was the artillery target and then a large number of projectiles were fired, and then sometimes only one or two shells were fired, and there was an effect to that too, of course, but, of course, there was no point to do that. But I'd really have to look this up if you're interested in the period from the 22th to the 30th, because I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, take a look at your chronology briefly and let's get a date as to when the shelling stopped in that area, if you can't recall, and we'll use the benchmark as the 30th of April and the frontal part being the 20th of April. So between the 20th and the 30th, when did it stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, were you able to look at your chronology?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a minute, please, because I have to look at ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We're going to take a break and give you the time to consult your chronology quietly. For 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume now. Please be seated. I want to say for the public that this is the cross-examination of General Blaskic who chose to testify and is under oath. Mr. Kehoe, you can continue with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we had an outstanding question on the floor of when the town of Vitez ceased being shelled.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have looked through my notes, and sometime from the 20th to the 30th, I haven't got any notes there on any more intensified shelling in the urban area of Vitez, but I do have notes saying that there was repeated sniper fire by the BH army and that there was shelling of the northern and southern lines of the front, so that the shelling increased on the northern and southern front lines of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General Blaskic. There's your answer, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of time from the 20th to the 30th when there was no intense shelling of downtown Vitez, the Bosnian Muslim prisoners continued to remain in the basement of the Workers' University and the cinema; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were in the cinema, and from the 20th onwards, from the period that you asked me about, that was the time when we worked towards establishing a joint command and a cease of hostilities and the work of joint commissions, according to the agreements of the 20th and 21st of April. At that time, we tried to stop all combat activities and to separate the forces and everything else following on from the Zenica agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if these prisoners were being used as human shields, the tactic worked, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were never used as human shields, nor is there one single order or document of any kind issued by me or my immediate subordinates on that. As far as I remember, I ordered in an order of the 18th of April that all prisoners be freed immediately but on the condition that the fighting had ceased and that the situation had been brought back to a safe one. I think that it would have been a far worse solution if all the people were turned out into the streets when fighting was still ongoing and when the situation was not safe which would enable these detained persons to be freed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you just said to us that "They were never used as human shields, nor is there one single order or document of any kind issued by me or my subordinates on that." There is also not one single order issued by you, after you knew that these civilians were in custody in the Dubravica school and in the Workers' University, to remove them from harm's way; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Already on the 17th of April, I issued an order, an express order of the 17th of April that civilians must be protected. On the 21st of April, I issued an order that my subordinates must, along with signatures of their subordinates, issue an order for full guarantee and protection of all civilians and that they must feed this information back to me, that is to say, that I receive it from the level of battalion commanders that they had received this order, that they are to issue full guarantee and protection to civilians. My order of the 18th of April was also along those lines, to free the civilians, but the problem was to ensure a cease-fire, to ensure that the situation was safe and secure. Let me say that one battalion of any army, for it to be able to take up defence positions, it needs three to six kilometres in depth. The broadest enclave was six kilometres, and then we could say -- we could put it this way: The position for the defence of the battalion, there is 75.000 people living there, if we look at the in-depth situation, that is to say, we are all in this position, and it wasn't safe for any civilian. I'm not thinking of any particular ethnicity but for all civilians living there. A brigade takes up positions in a depth of 35 kilometres, and we didn't have that depth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I understand that the people who were in the Vitez cinema, I've understood you saying that these people in the cinema were saying that you would protect them. Did you consider that you were responsible for their safety when they were in the Vitez cinema, or that's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, I consider that it was not possible and that it was far less secure to leave these people out in the streets in conditions where there had not been a halt to the fighting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But did you give them that choice? Did you ask them the question? Did you give them a choice? Are you the one who decided that their safety would be ensured by going into the cinema; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the course of the day, Mr. President, they went home, some to have a shower, some to change clothes, some to have something to eat, but I ordered on the 18th of April that they all be set free; however, this order of the 18th of April had two preconditions: the cessation of hostilities and the creation of safe positions. So I don't maintain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you made a choice for them; you set the conditions. You made choices for them; you set conditions for their being released?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, those were the conditions that I knew about from the International Red Cross, that is to say, any individual can be freed only if there is no more fighting and if the situation is safe for them to be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But let's not have the International Red Cross speak, and it's not here to speak for itself. Perhaps it would have been satisfied if you did release them. Let's not put words into the mouth of the International Red Cross. You set those conditions. It seems to me that you are the one who set those two conditions.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received this kind of order from General Petkovic on the basis of an agreement reached between President Izetbegovic and Boban. So they had received a military and political agreement, and I received an order for a cessation of hostilities and the release of civilians and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to ask. Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I hear you speaking about safety or security when you speak about detention. If we're speaking about security, were the security conditions different for the Croats and the Muslims? In other words, the Muslims were in the Vitez cinema and the Croats were at home. From the point of view of security, could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I already said that I found out that the Muslims were being brought in, that is to say, I did not order it and I did not ask that they be brought into custody. But then when I was surprised to hear that they were being kept at the cinema, then I thought that the best thing would be to work for a cease-fire, for creating safe conditions, and then for their release. The situation was similar where the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Vitez was in charge of a particular area. I imagine that it was the same. Muslim Bosniaks were deployed in certain places, and Croats were brought to certain buildings and temporarily kept in these buildings because in that kind of a situation, it's difficult to have control over everything that goes on in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But in respect of the conditions that you're speaking about, were those conditions transmitted to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The agreement was reached by the two top men, Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban. I think this was on the 17th or 18th of April, the agreement on the cessation of hostilities and releases and everything else that was supposed to take place. I received orders from General Petkovic, and I sent a copy of the order that I had written to the 3rd Corps, and I read the order issued by General Petkovic to the duty officer of the 3rd Corps over the telephone. I'm sure that he wrote down all the conditions because I heard his voice. But these were orders issued by the two commanders, that is to say, the chief of the general staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, if the agreement was reached on the 17th, why was detention extended until the 30th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first agreement was on the 16th of April, and it was not observed; then on the 17th of April, it was not observed; on the 18th, it was not observed; on the 20th in Zenica, it was. Then the decision was that the release of all persons would be handled by civilian commissions under the leadership of the International Red Cross. I can give you my assessment, why so much time had to go by. There are three reasons, in my opinion: One is to have a cease-fire and safe conditions, and the second reason was that the International Red Cross asked to have some kind of an interview or test or discussion with each detainee so that they could get the personal details of the detainees and also hear where these persons wanted to go after they were released. So there were problems in obtaining lists, but these were problems related to the commissions for release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But if you say, General Blaskic, that only you released the prisoners if there was an agreement, at the end you used the detainees in order to put pressure on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm not saying that I would release the prisoners. I never conditionally issued such an order, nor did I ever think in that way. I'm just saying that in the January conflict, I was a witness of the attitude and conclusion of the International Red Cross in which the International Red Cross defined the conditions and possibilities for the release. I think that the order from the 18th of April is there, and I never put forth as a precondition a cease-fire so that I would release all the prisoners as if it were my own precondition, no, and I was never the creator of any agreement, no. My superiors were discussing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I'm getting a little lost here. I wonder if you can help me. Do I understand you to be saying that the position is this: No decision by you for the release of any detained persons could be implemented without going through certain Red Cross procedures? Was that the position?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what we did from the January conflict onwards, Your Honour. I never thought that I had the sole right to write an order saying that persons could simply be released just like that without having full insight by the International Red Cross, that is to say, that they could register these persons, interview them, take their personal details, see where they wanted to go afterwards, et cetera, and then when the Red Cross officers thought that the conditions had been created for that, at a meeting this person would take the floor and say, "Yes, these conditions have been met," and there's going to be release under such and such conditions. That's the way we always did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So that if you decided today that certain people should be released, and if it took another six weeks to go through the Red Cross procedures, that person could not be released until those procedures had been completed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my notes, Your Honour, I certainly have this written down very precisely. I think that this was Mr. Fleming's viewpoint, from February 1993, when he decided that the release, mutual release, of detained persons be carried out immediately. Then this conclusion was presented to myself and Mr. Merdan, I think. After that, Mrs. Iris called. She was a representative of the International Red Cross. She had an office in Zenica, and she was in charge of the Zenica region. She said that she believed that not all the conditions had been created for the release to take place. Then we bowed to the attitude of the lady representative of the International Red Cross. Whenever there were releases, it was the International Red Cross that dictated the conditions, when and how the release would take place, and they intermediated and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me show you the Defence 316, please, and if we could also pull out Defence 318, please. Now, General, in Defence Exhibit 316, you were ordered by Milivoj Petkovic, on the 18th of April, 1993, to -- can you put that on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher? You were ordered to: "2. The exchange of prisoners, both soldiers and civilians, shall start immediately." In Defence Exhibit 318, we have the English version of the order that you sent copying Petkovic's order which is based on an agreement between Mate Boban, between Boban and Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could put 318 on the ELMO now, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, General, you had the authority on the 18th to release civilians from custody, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said how I understood this authority. If necessary, I can repeat that. On the 17th already an agreement had been reached, on the 17th or 18th, I'm not sure, concerning the exchange of detainees. However, the problem was the cease-fire, and the creation of safe conditions and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Excuse me, General. The question is: Did you have the authority to release prisoners as of the 18th of April, to release them so they could go back and live with their Bosnian Croat neighbours? Did you have that authority?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had to honour the protocol of the International Red Cross, and I asked my subordinates to do that too. That is what the prevailing practice was, that is to say, although I had issued an order, the attitude of the International Red Cross had to be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But that's not what it says in the order. Well, continue, Mr. Kehoe. I don't think that's what it says in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's exactly the point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what the order says, does it, General, neither Petkovic's order, nor your order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that there is a procedure and a protocol for the release of prisoners, and I was duty-bound to honour the protocol of the International Red Cross. I worked in the faith that I was observing that protocol. In this order that you're asking me about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I'm not saying that you didn't do it. I'm not taking sides. In respect to the Prosecutor's question, I just simply wanted to point that in number 2 in the paragraph it says that an exchange of prisoners must be effected immediately. That's what your superior said, Milivoj Petkovic. The word "immediately" there should be an exchange of military and civilian prisoners he did not add, "In accordance with an agreement we take, get into contact with the Croats." That's all I'm saying. I'm not saying anything beyond that. I'm not asking any questions. The Prosecutor has to prove what he's putting forth, but in order to save some time, I would like you to answer the questions very specifically. Is says in Petkovic's order that an exchange of civilian and military prisoners should be carried out immediately. That's all it says, "Yes" or "No"? Then, of course, you can say what you like.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll try to be as brief as possible. That's what it says in the document and that's what it says in document 318, I believe. However, we always observe the protocol of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. That's your answer. I respect your answer, but I wanted to be sure that we had both read the same document. All right. Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we heard the testimony of Sefik Pezer that was released on the 30th of April, 1993, but there were other Bosnian Muslims that were kept in custody until the 8th or 10th of May of 1993; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said from the 20th of April the release of all detainees was taken over by the commission consisting of two representatives. On the one side was a Croat, on the other side was a Bosniak Muslim, and it was chaired by a representative of the International Red Cross. How fast persons were released, that I don't have information about because the commission was not subordinated to me but to the governmental commission that belonged to the civilian authorities of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were they held in custody, General? How long were these civilians, these Bosnian Muslim civilians, kept in custody?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have the exact information on how the exchange took place, because I already said that the commission on releases and exchanges was under the authority of the civilian authorities and this was carried out in accordance with the International Red Cross. Releases were two sided, that is to say, of Bosniak Muslims and of Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it your testimony that the Bosnian Muslims in the cinema and in Dubravica school were free to leave when they wanted to? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that Bosniak Muslims from the cinema would go home to take a shower. Somebody would go to take lunch at home and others had their lunch brought to them and, also, some members of the Vitez Brigade would take some of them home by car. There were such cases. So what the conditions were like, well, I did not receive any information concerning inhumane treatment of these persons. I never received such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We agree that some would go home to take a shower and come back in the evening voluntarily? Do we agree that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what I was being told, that some of them would go home to have lunch at home, or some had their lunch brought to them at the cinema. So there were such cases too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, why would they return from their homes to the cinema? Would they return voluntarily or would their return because they were told that they had to return? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to assess this now. I can only assume that probably every one of them was perhaps warned that they should come back. Perhaps there were cases when they thought that they were safer there, it was safer to stay there than at home. It's hard for me to judge that, because high-quality safety conditions had not been created yet to guarantee the full safety of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, the situation was, was it not, that the men periodically were told to go home and come back, while their wives remained at their homes in Vitez while they were in custody in the cinema; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were such cases too, or their wives would bring them food from home. There were such cases too. Or some of the people from headquarters would take some of their neighbours from there to their own homes. So I heard of such information, and I didn't hear of any inhumane treatment of these detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that, General. I mean, you would agree, based on what you just told us and told Judge Shahabuddeen, that these Bosnian Muslim civilians were not free to come and go and do as they pleased; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: To do as they pleased? Well, they certainly weren't free in the proper sense of the word, but they were -- but it was on the way to have mutual release both ways, but the situation was such that for a given period of time it was perhaps the safest to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, while these civilians were kept in the cinema, which is 30 and 40 yards away from your headquarters, and kept in the Dubravica school, the Bosnian Muslim men were taken out to dig trenches by HVO troops under your command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already said that I never approved of such activity, nor did I ever order it. I was aware of individual cases of such activity, and I reacted by way of investigations and by way of prohibiting direct orders that would entail such behaviour. On the 20th of April, and even earlier, an order had been issued that detainees had to be respected and had to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the reality or the fact is, General, that you knew that Bosnian Muslim civilians were being taken from the cinema and brought to the front lines to dig trenches, and they were brought to the front lines to dig trenches by your troops; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that there were individual cases when persons were taken out, and there was information to that effect. This was as far back as in February, and that is when I started an investigation in this respect. I prohibited this kind of activity, and I prohibited it in the same way in April, on the 20th of April I prohibited this, and my position was that a soldier had to dig his own shelter, and that can be seen from my documents from September 1992. There were individual cases when people were taken out, and I tried to stop this because this was in contravention of my orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you ever take the 30-yard to 40-yard trip from your headquarters and go examine the conditions under which those Bosnian Muslim civilians were kept in the cinema? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had many meetings. I did not go simply because I had never received any information from the International Red Cross or from my associates that they were being treated inhumanely, that is to say, I did not have such information. At that time, I was working on activities related to the cease-fire and the implementation of the agreement that we had reached in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never personally examined whether or not these civilians were being mistreated or misfed, nor did you ask any of them if, in fact, they had been forced to do labour on the front lines for the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally did not carry out investigations because I had assistants who would take care of that, and I also had my subordinates who would inform me about this, that is to say, that I did not receive information that they were being treated inhumanely, and I did not go to visit them and I did not react. I only did in situations, as I already said, when I had received such information, and then I would request an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Defence 365, General, which is your order of the 27th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, before you turn to that exhibit, could you help me with one area of some perplexity to me? I gather from what you said that some Bosnian Muslim men who were detained at this cinema would go home for a shower and would then return to the cinema out of a preference for the greater security which the cinema afforded them, but they would leave their wives at home. How do you reconcile the latter with the former? How do you reconcile their preference for the security of the cinema with their leaving their wives behind at home exposed, presumably? Could you help me with that problem?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Regrettably, Your Honour, at that time, there were quite a few private arrests as well that I have already spoken about, that is to say, that if an HVO member had been arrested, then a group or the relatives of that person would take into their own custody a member of the BH army or a conscript or someone, and then they would engage in these private exchanges, I'm sure that there was that problem, and then the existence of units that were out of control and others that could also engage in such efforts, that is, private exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We've now received D365 from the registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, in D365, you send an order to the Viteska Brigade commander, and in number 1, you say: "1. I prohibit any treatment of temporarily detained civilians which is contrary to the basic provisions of the Geneva Convention." Now, General, if there was no mistreatment of these prisoners, why did you specifically send this to Mario Cerkez, the commander of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that it is possible that there were individual cases. This order is not the first order of this kind. I think that my first order was issued before that, and there's a document from the 21st of April, 1993 where I asked for full safety to be provided for civilians in the territory of the municipality of Vitez. This was the 21st of April. Then this is a supplement to the order issued on the 24th of April, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the individual cases that you just discussed of mistreatment of prisoners, did you punish those violators? If you did, what did you do and to whom did you mete this punishment out?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me just look it up in my notes, please. If the information reached me and if it was under my competency, I did discipline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us narrow the question then. Do you have the name of one HVO soldier that you disciplined for abusing a civilian who was detained at the cinema? One name.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received information, I think it was from the Vitez Brigade, on the 14th of May, 1993, an incident that took place previously towards Hasan Gerdijanovic, and this incident was caused by the members of the HVO, Vlado Lesic, Bozo and Zeljko Babic and Zvonko Bilic. They were the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. That was not the question I asked you. The question I asked you is do you have the name of one HVO soldier who was disciplined for abusing Bosnian Muslim civilians who were held at the cinema?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You didn't let the witness finish, Mr. Kehoe. I suppose that the witness wanted to mention an incident that happened in May, not in April. I think that now you're going to tell us that after the incident, you took some sanctions against somebody, and I suppose you're going to give us the name; is that right, Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. On that occasion, I was informed about an incident which had taken place previously, so that particular individual, Hasan Gerdijanovic, was imprisoned, and this group of men provoked him, the group that I named earlier on. I demanded that they be sent away from the unit and that disciplinary measures be taken. The group was identified, that is to say, they were Vlado Lesic, Bozo and Zeljko Babic, and Zvonko Bilic. Those were the perpetrators, and that was what I did on the basis of a report that I received from the commander of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question goes back to prisoners that were held in custody in the cinema, and my question for you is this: Were any HVO soldiers disciplined for abusing Bosnian Muslims who were held captive in the cinema? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, General Blaskic? Try to answer it, about the cinema.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am saying, on the basis of my recollections, that probably there was a meeting between one prisoner in the cinema, that is to say, Mr. Hasan Gerdijanovic, and this incident when one of these individuals mentioned either pushed him away or cursed him or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you sure that's in the cinema? Are you sure that that took place in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're under oath, I remind you, General Blaskic. You just added that yes, it was in the cinema. Are you sure that it was in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am sure -- I am sure that I received information that it was an incident that had taken place in the cinema. So that is the information that I received from my subordinates. That is what I'm certain of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, ask your question, please. Let's move things forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question on the cinema, General. Was any HVO soldier disciplined for taking Bosnian Muslim civilians to the front lines to dig trenches from the cinema?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That kind of activity represented a criminal act, and in concrete terms, the cinema, I know that an investigation was undertaken in one particular case, but I do not know the punishment and the course the proceedings took of that particular case. I think it was a case where somebody ended up dead and people who had taken this person trench digging were disciplined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you, of course, are referring to the incident in February, and I am referring to the trench digging in April and May. Do you have a name of an HVO soldier disciplined or punished by the courts for forcing Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches at the front lines when they had been incarcerated in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that it was my position that I ban such acts and that I remember that an incident had taken place where they had been taken from the cinema to trench digging and that one individual died, one prisoner ended up dead, and that that case was investigated and proceedings taken at court. I haven't got the names of the individuals in question responsible for the incident and what the results of the punishment meted out by the military district court were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, General. Thank you. We will move on to another subject. I would like to move back to the individuals, the civilians from Gacice. We had talked about those civilians previously being taken down to the Hotel Vitez, and I'm talking about the 247 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just go into private session briefly on this matter, Mr. President, because there is some testimony I would like to refer to that was taken in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will that take a long time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It's very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wanted the public to know that sometimes there are closed sessions which take quite a bit of time. All right. We're going to go into private session now. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I'd like to review with you briefly these 12 photographs which you can examine on the ELMO, and if we can, Mr. Usher. These are photographs taken by the British Battalion several days after the truck bomb explosion in Stari Vitez. This is, of course, 525/1. The next one. This is 525/2. The next one, please. 525/3. General, you can examine them on the ELMO if you want to, sir. 525/4, 525/5, 525/6, 525/7, 525/8, 525/9, 525/10, 525/11, and 525/12. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Now, General, this is an explosion in Stari Vitez that took place approximately 400 metres from your headquarters at the Hotel Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps that was the distance but I don't know exactly. Perhaps that was the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to read you a portion of the testimony of Brigadier Slavko Marin, on page 13433 and 434. The question was asked on line 24 of page 13433: "Q Would you agree with me, Brigadier, that what happened in this truck bomb was an act of terrorism, wasn't it? A Yes. This is a very ugly act and an act which no army could resort to in its conduct." General, do you agree with the sentiments expressed by your chief of staff at that time and your chief of operations?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, let us examine the level of this detonation first. If I could give this exhibit out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 706, Prosecution Exhibit 706.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
