utterances.text: Mr. President, just by way of explanation on this exhibit and the legend annexed thereto, the various statements that we have of witness Colonel Martin Thomas, Captain Tudor Ellis, Lieutenant Colonel Henk Morsink, and Advija Hrustic are designated by the letters on the maps A through D respectively, but it's also the location in which they were, as well as the lines of the transcript that verify their location when the explosion actually took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, just examining this particular map, the first location is Colonel Thomas, now Colonel Thomas, who is at location A which is the British Battalion camp, and the question asked him by my colleague Mr. Cayley, on page 2589, at line 14: "Q I think you returned to the Stari Bila camp and now I want to take you forward in time to the 18th and 19th of April. I think it was whilst you were in the camp at Stari Bila that you heard a very large explosion; is that right? A Yes. I think it was Sunday evening, getting dark, and we heard an enormous bang coming from the centre of Vitez and, again, as we were at that time the Ops Company, I was sent down -- at that time I went with 2 Platoon, so we went down with five Warriors." Moving to the next person on the map, who is Captain Tudor Ellis, who was in Sivrino Selo, and he notes at page 3011, line 13: "Q What did you feel? A I was in my vehicle and we had stopped. We had seen the green car disappear, and I remember feeling that this big force, this shock wave hit me. At the same time a huge bang, a massive explosion. I looked down to where the bang had come from and there was a huge plume of smoke rising from the town of Vitez. I remember at the time we had a patrol in the town who reported that there had been a massive explosion. There were large amount of casualties, and they needed callsigns in the town as quickly as possible. Q How far were you from Vitez at the time? A I was about two kilometres again, in the village of Sivrino Selo." The next locale is the locale of Colonel Morsink who was in Gornja Rovna, and he is in locale 3 -- excuse me, C. He is on page 9820, who notes that, on line 23: "A When the bomb exploded, I was with the ECMM team in a place that was called Gornja Rovna which was five kilometres away from the centre of Vitez. Gornja Rovna is on the hill and from it you can see Vitez very clearly. When we would have a discussion with the local commanders on the front line, we could see that there was artillery fire on the neighbouring hills, and all of a sudden, I think it was at the end of the afternoon around 5.00, when I heard an enormous explosion in Vitez. We saw that there was smoke, there was a huge cloud of smoke that was rising, and at that time we did not react." The last person on the list is Advija Hrustic, at point D in Gacice, who notes on page 4805, line 13: "A We heard the shelling, the fire, and there was a very powerful explosion. One had the feeling that the house was coming down. On my house the glass, together with the frame, came down and a balcony door also fell to the floor from the explosion. The house was shaking as if it was going to tumble down. All glass panes in the surrounding houses were broken." That is point D. So, General, you would agree, would you not, that this was the most powerful explosion that took place in the Vitez area during the course of the hostilities; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was the most powerful explosion, although there was another explosion in October, I think it was, 1993, but not in the town of Vitez, in the position at Zabrdze, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree, sir, that what happened in Stari Vitez at approximately 5.00 on the 18th of April, 1993, was a war crime?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about some other testimony, if we can, beginning with the testimony of Dr. Mujenznovic. If I may hand out another exhibit prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This, Mr. President -- I will wait until the copies are handed out before an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know that we're going until 6.00 this evening. We should take another break. When would you like to take the break? What seems to be the most consistent with what you're doing in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Any time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we should take a 15-minute break now then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. I think that the break could be used in order to distribute the Prosecutor's documents which means that the Prosecutor can begin immediately and continue until 6.00, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Actually, that was my negligence with one exhibit that I didn't give, unfortunately, to the registrar, and I apologise to the registrar for that, but it was a larger exhibit which is an expansion of the particular exhibit that we have. So I do apologise for not doing that promptly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The big map will be 707 as a Prosecution Exhibit and it will have a copy in reduced form which will be 707/1. We're going to distribute that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you going to use the same method, that is, these are excerpts of reports of testimonies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, same methodology, Mr. President. On these five locales, we will just go through them briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You tried to summarise things so that we can move along more quickly. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This has to do with those who knew of this truck bomb explosion prior to the actual explosion taking place, and we will be moving in chronological order from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first individual is Dr. Fuad Zeco who was in custody in the veterinarian station on the 18th of April, 1993 at approximately 5.00. His testimony reflects that: "A ... But at that point, the same person came in, this person who organised this prison of ours, Zeljko Matkovic --" By the way, I'm reading, I'm sorry, at page 2815: "A ... Zeljko Matkovic, and he said, 'all of you, each and every one of you should go to the basement and that is it. Something is going to happen now.' He said that we had to go to the basement. We were curious, we were surprised, wondering what it was. It was not clear at all, but he specifically asked us to hurry and to go down to the basement. The staircase was narrow, and those people who got downstairs had to make room for others, so we were not moving at the speed they wanted. Nevertheless, we all did manage to get down and we huddled in there, it might be a room 3 metres by 6 to 7 metres, and a few moments after we got down there, we felt an explosion which was really strong. There had been explosions until then too, but none of them matched this one. It was long, it was strong, and to the best of our knowledge, it was pretty far away, but it was something big." The later question on page 2869, this is at line 25: "Q Zeljko Matkovic who, as you said, was some kind of a commander, to which unit did he belong to in the HVO?" The witness didn't know what unit and said: "A I do not know ..." The next one we have as we move down, Mr. President, is number 2, and this is Dr. Mujezinovic who, in Exhibit 45B circled the area that he lived, and that's in the area of Vitez called Kolonija. That is designated as number 2 on the map. He notes on page 1697, question on line 15: "Q At some point in time, while you were in your apartment building, did you receive a warning of some kind? A Yes, on Sunday around 5.00, Katava Marinko warned us we were not allowed to go out anywhere, because in the hallway there were local people with arms. They were mostly wearing civilian clothes, some of them were in camouflage uniforms with rifles, and we did not move anywhere. Then Marinko Katava warned me and my neighbours, or rather my wife, my children, my in-laws -- he did not talk much to me -- that we should not be afraid, that a strong explosion would be heard." Turning to page 1698, line 14: "Q Was there, in fact, a powerful explosion that occurred shortly thereafter? A It was dusk. First there was a powerful light and then a very strong explosion. We did not know what it was and then Marinko Katava said, 'Do not be afraid. We have hit Djuda's ammunition depot,' as he put it, and Dzevada Topcic, known as Djuda, held in Stari Vitez a warehouse, and he claimed that an ammunition depot in Stari Vitez had been blown up and that that was the explosion." The next one is C, and that is Sefik Pezer. Mr. Pezer testified that when the explosion went off, he was in the Vitez cinema building as a prisoner. That is on page 1573, line 19: "Q Mr. Pezer, after you were in the cinema for several days, did you have a conversation with any military policemen concerning an explosion or shelling that he said was going to take place, and if that did happen, can you explain it to the judges? A Are you thinking of the cistern that went off in Stari Vitez? Q Yes, sir. A On that day, a soldier, an HVO soldier, came to the basement. I was in the basement at the time, and we used the toilet which was on the ground floor of the building, and as there were a lot of us we would come and go. We would go to the hall where the toilet was, and then the soldier came and said, 'No one should go out because we are expecting some heavy shelling', so that nobody would get hit. Only a little while after that, we heard a powerful explosion. We knew immediately that it was not any shelling, because the explosion was very powerful. It was nothing like a grenade or any other device of that kind." The next person is Witness E, and Witness E did have protective measures, Mr. President, but she did testify in open session. She testified concerning the warning, and she is living at point 4, which, as we can see from the exhibit on the right-hand side, was depicted in Prosecutor's Exhibit 45E. This begins on page 2912, line 21, she noted: "A ... We were terrified for our husbands and our fathers. One day there was some sort of an alert in the basement. Women, Croat women, were talking and one woman whose husband, a Croat, had to go to another part of the Kolonija. She called me and another neighbour, a Muslim, and she was closer to the telephone because in the meantime all the telephones were cut." If we move down on line 4 of page 2913: "A ... she said that something was being prepared, an explosion or something, and she had left her keys so that we could use them and that we should open the windows, because there might be an explosion." Line 14 of the same page: "A Anyway, when I entered the corridor of my apartment, I do not know what came first, the sound of the explosion or the dust that was choking me in my nose and mouth. So I ran down to see whether the children were alive, whether there was any destruction. At first, we did not know what it was. Later on, when I went to visit my husband, as women were coming from all over Kolonija, we learnt that there had been an explosion in Stari Vitez." On page 2914 at line 8: "A She said that, if we could, we should go to her apartment and to our own apartment to open the windows, because something terrible was in the offing, that we should not risk anything and that we should stay in the basement because something would happen." Question on line 20 of 2914: "Q What had these Croat women learned from the radio and the TV?" If I can back up on line 13: "Q In the basement, were the Croat women talking to one another about something during this period of time? A Yes, they were talking. I later learnt that they had also heard on the radio and the TV, because in the meantime a TV set and a radio had been brought down to the basement, because we spent eight nights and nine days in the basement. Q What had these Croat women learned from the radio and the TV? A I do not know exactly. I think their husbands could have told them too, because another neighbour had moved away to another building. She also called up another neighbour saying that something was going to happen, that her husband had told her that and her husband was a HVO soldier. Q But it clear, Witness E, that all of these people knew that some type of large explosion was going to take place before it happened? A Yes, maybe even two hours before it happened. I do not know exactly how it happened, we were all very afraid, but much earlier, anyhow." The last witness is a Defence witness, Mr. President, Marijan Strukar, which is at number 5, who lived south of Stari Vitez, and it is in the area of number 5. Mr. Strukar, on page 16833 notes that -- excuse me, on that page, he notes the approximate location of his home, and on page 16884, at line 21, he notes: "Q Yes, and would you please explain the symbols you used to denote the Croat houses and the Muslim houses?" And he picks his house, saying: "A This is my house here (indicating), and the Muslim houses I have marked in the following way." [Page 16933]: "A ... houses where civilians were housed. We would go and have something to eat and drink. At one point in the house in which I was located, one of the men up there came into the house and told us to take refuge because there would be a loud explosion. Q Who told you this? A Somebody, that man that came to the house. There was information from all sides, and at this particular point, a man walked in and told us not to leave the house, not to leave the premises, because there would be a strong explosion. And, yes, indeed, three to four minutes later, there was a terrible explosion which shattered the windows of the houses." The question on cross on page 16991 of Mr. Strukar, line 9: "Q My question was: Who was it who warned you about the bomb? A I can't remember because, as I say, we weren't just sitting there and somebody came up to us to tell us something. It was just somebody shouting. For example, I would like to say something that isn't appropriate for this court, and they would just say, 'Get the hell out of there. Get inside. Get inside.' So that they thought that something might be happening." Now, General, you noted for us that you had no knowledge about the detonation of the truck bomb prior to that detonation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's not only that I didn't know about it before the detonation took place, but I didn't even know about it during the detonation itself. I know that at that time I recorded this as the hotel being hit, and we thought that the hotel had been hit with a 122 millimetre mortar, and we were in the basement of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we had testimony that some of the information came from HVO soldiers and other information came from an individual by the name of Marinko Katava. Do you know Marinko Katava?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I met him when he arrived in detention. I didn't know him before that. I never knew him before that. I never met him before that. I first met him here in The Hague detention unit, but if I heard about his testimony well, then that coincides with what I received from the Vitez Brigade, that is to say, that the warehouse was hit, either Vitkom Borac. That is a warehouse of ammunition and explosives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Marinko Katava a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a member of the HVO, because there were perhaps 10.000 members of the HVO. I never knew him before. I had never heard of him before he came to The Hague detention unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, how is it possible that the HVO soldiers at the cinema, guarding prisoners, HVO soldiers guarding prisoners at the veterinary school, individuals in apartments in Kolonija, both north and south Kolonija, and we're talking about Dr. Mujenznovic, and Witness E, and even a Defence witness, Marijan Strukar, all these people knew that this detonation was going to take place and you didn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's not a question, that's argument. It's not a question, it's just argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's not argument at all, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you at all, Mr. Hayman. It is a question. I don't agree with you. First of all, the form is a question, it is interrogative. That is, how is it that some people know? That's a question. I'm sorry. The Prosecutor has the right to ask it, and I would invite the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time I was in the basement and the only communications I could have was via the telephone and it was only on the telephone that I could receive information. I did not receive such information at any point in time, even that there would be an explosion. When the explosion actually took place, I know we recorded it as the hotel being hit by artillery fire. Later, when we contacted the Vitez Brigade, we heard that the warehouse in Stari Vitez was hit. This is on the other side of the front line, that is to say, under BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, General, was this publicised on the TV and the radio in Vitez that, in fact, an explosion like this was going to take place?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. At that time I was in the basement of the hotel. I didn't watch television. I didn't listen to the radio. I don't know about this at all, because at that time -- well, my activities were there from one minute to another, and I didn't really hear such information. I didn't even listen. This is the first time I ever hear of this, this claim of yours. I don't know if any of my associates knowing about it either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, you were in communication with Mario Cerkez and other individuals in the Vitez area during this period of time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I communicated with Mario Cerkez on the telephone most often, and every one of these communications is in my operative diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a military man, would you also assume that Mario Cerkez was in communication with his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, to the extent possible, that is to say, as much as he could have under the circumstances. I believe that he was in communication with his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the bottom line, General, is that women and children in the basement of a building in Kolonija were better informed about the situation than you were. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received information from my immediate subordinates, and I acted on the basis of that information. Whether somebody had more or less information than I did, I cannot be the judge of that, but on the basis of the information I received, I could act only on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the information you received from the Vitez Brigade. Exhibit 304. Defence Exhibit 304, excuse me. Now, General, this is your report that we have discussed. You discussed this at some length on direct-examination with my colleague Mr. Nobilo. General, this reflects that it was the detonation of a quantity of explosives in Stari Vitez that caused the bomb. Now, General, when were you informed that it was, in fact, a truck bomb that went off in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly when this took place. At any rate, I remember that later on, information -- we received information that it was a truck bomb, but I cannot remember when this was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you'd like to look at your chronology you can, but it's a very specific question. When did you receive the information about the truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I don't know whether this is entered in my chronology. I can look it up, but I cannot remember exactly when I received that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Continue, please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you some testimony by Mr. Morsink -- Lieutenant Colonel Morsink, questions by my colleague, Mr. Harmon. This is on page 9822 "Q Now, Colonel Morsink, the next day, the 19th of April, 1993, was the matter raised? Was the issue of the truck bomb and the explosion in a civilian area of Stari Vitez raised with local military and political figures? A In the morning of the 19th of April, the HVO Vitez Brigade commander, Mr. Mario Cerkez, in his office I brought up the subject together with my monitor colleague, Pedersen. I remember that Mr. Pedersen said that this was not a normal thing that one would do in a war, that it was really a terrorist act, and I remember that shortly afterwards somebody from the meeting came who was outside the meeting. He introduced himself as Mr. Anto Valenta. He had a political function in the region, I don't quite remember which one exactly it was, but I think that it was -- it was the -- he was the vice-president of the HDZ. When Mr. Valenta came in, we went back to the issue of the truck bomb, and Mr. Valenta, like Mr. Cerkez, recounted the event as they saw it. I remember Mr. Valenta said that there had been a munitions depot which had been hit by a shell and that was why the truck exploded. Mr. Cerkez explained the things to us somewhat differently. He said that the truck had been hit by a grenade or by firing, and I remember my colleague, Pedersen, insisted on the fact that this was not a sufficient explanation. He insisted by saying that an investigation needed to be carried out, and Cerkez stated that he would do so." Now, General, you would agree, would you not, that the information that Mario Cerkez gave to Colonel Morsink on the 19th was significantly different than the information that he gave to you in a report that we have, Defence Exhibit 304?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, because this is the 18th of April, 1993 at 18.45. So Mario Cerkez probably gave information on the 18th of April, 1993 at 18.45, that is to say, the kind of information that he had. On the 19th of April, he probably learned new things and I imagine that's the way it was. But on the basis of this report that he gave on the 18th of April, 1993, it is quite obvious that he speaks about the explosion of the warehouse. I think that Katava mentioned this too, if I listened carefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, did Cerkez tell you about this truck bomb on the 19th? Did he give you the information that he gave to Lieutenant Colonel Morsink?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot specifically remember who told me that it was a truck bomb, but I know that after that, after having received such information, I requested an investigation from the security service about this truck bomb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this was a terrorist act 400 metres away from your headquarters, and is it your testimony you do not specifically recall when someone told you what the source of this terrorist act was?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is correct that this is 400 metres away from my headquarters, but it is also correct that it is on the other side, that is to say, behind the front line. This position was held by the BH army, and I cannot specifically recall the details, who told me, but I know at one point in time I found out too that this was a truck bomb. I didn't learn about all the details, and I asked the security service to carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, what was your reaction when you heard about this terrorist act?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I already said that I asked the assistant for security to start an investigation and to provide me with all the information that he had about this activity, that is to say, about everything that had happened and everything else, under which circumstances this happened and who the suspects were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me narrow that question a little bit more, General. Were you angry? Were you upset? Were you outraged at this terrorist act? What was your reaction as a human being?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, of course I was surprised by this activity, and I was astonished by this activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me read you some testimony from Colonel Morsink on page 9824. Question on line 4: "Q Let me ask you, the next day, on the 20th of April, 1993, were you at a meeting with Colonel Stewart, Clare Podbielski, who was from ICRC, and Colonel Blaskic, where the incident of the truck bomb was raised? A Yes, I was present. I was in the headquarters. It was at the Hotel Vitez, and I remember it was the first time that I was in that particular headquarters building. I also remember quite well that Mr. Bob Stewart was also quite excited. He was furious. He was furious to see that the HVO were not reacting after this truck exploded. He was also furious because the Croats had accused the British of having participated or to have been active in that event because there were only Muslims that were wounded and also -- only the Muslims, rather, were being evacuated by them. He protested very strongly. Q What was Colonel Blaskic's reaction to those protests? A I recall he was listening but he didn't make any objections. He simply listened to the statements made by Stewart, nor did he exclude the possibility of an investigation, but nor did he really react." Line 18, 9825: "Q Was Colonel Blaskic fully aware of the truck bomb explosion, where it had occurred and that there was a demand for an investigation into that event? A Yes. That happened a few days earlier, not more than a kilometre from his headquarters. Q So the explosion could be heard from five kilometres away? A Of course, yes." Now, General, you were informed of this truck bomb at least by Colonel Stewart on the 20th of April, 1993, were you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that I did not meet with Mr. Morsink, with Colonel Stewart, and with Clare Podbielski from the International Red Cross on the 20th of April, 1993. I do not have this date recorded at all in any of my notes, and I know that had I met any one of these officials, I would have recorded that. On the 21st I had my first meeting in Zenica in relation to negotiations. Secondly, I first saw photographs of the explosion here in this courtroom, and that's the first time that I tried to recognise where this had happen. Before that I only had information that it was on the other side of the front line, under BH army control, but on the 20th of April I have all the meetings that I had recorded, at least the date and the contents, but I did not meet these officials. Later on there was a meeting with Colonel Stewart and Clare Podbielski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, when did you give this investigation to SIS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Immediately after I realised that this was a truck bomb, I asked the SIS assistant to find out exactly what had happened. Possibly this was the 19th, or the 20th, or the 21st, or the 22nd. I'm not sure of the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to your recollection, the time when you learned about the truck bomb was somewhere between the 19th and the 22nd of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Possibly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, had you given this investigation to the military police, the military police, of course, would have been obliged to give you their final report, isn't that right, as this was a routine police matter?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. I said that I asked the assistant for security to provide me with a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Listen to my question. Had you asked the military police for a report on the facts, the military police would have been obliged to give you that report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most of the investigations that I requested I requested from the security assistant, because the military police is directly subordinated to the military police administration, and they submitted most reports according to their own line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Listen to my question and I will repeat it again. My question is: Had you asked the military police for a report on the facts, the military police would have been obliged to give you that report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A report on the investigation, on the findings of the investigation, the military police submits to the administration of military police, as far as I know, and if the case has been closed, then a criminal report is filed with the district military court. They are not directly subordinated to me, and they didn't have to submit that report to me, that is to say, that this report did not have to be submitted to me, to the best of my knowledge at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it now your testimony that the military police is not subordinated to you for routine police tasks? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Daily operative police tasks, yes, the military police is subordinated to me for that. However, when crimes are concerned and investigations of crimes, then also this is done on the basis of the Law on Criminal Procedure, and the military police cooperates together with the civilian police and the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the normal course of business, you get a copy of this report as the commander of the Operative Zone, and you can decide whether or not you're going to discipline a particular soldier or you're going to possibly refer this information to the district military prosecutor; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If it is a crime, then it is compulsory to submit a criminal report if the names of the perpetrators are known. The district military prosecutor decides whether there are going to be criminal proceedings or disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We've already spoken about Article 29 of the decree. The Judges are familiar with your interpretation. Let's move forward. Who was asked to do the investigation, your assistant, your assistant for security?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the assistant for security who was in charge of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I would only like to ask you whether your assistant for security was your subordinate or not.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not directly subordinated to me. He's subordinated to the security administration from Mostar. Also, the chief of military police is not directly subordinated to me but to the administration from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. Are we going to know who was asked to carry out the report and whether there was an investigation? Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, who was it in SIS that you asked to assist to carry out this investigation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The security assistant, Ante Sliskovic, who was at that time assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Sliskovic tell you that he found out it was the Vitezovi who were behind the truck bomb and that the information had been sent to Mostar? When did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was a few days later, but I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we have approximation? Would it be the 24th, 25th, 26th of April? Would it be prior to May 1st, just to give us approximation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was approximately in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a little bit closer? The early part of May, the latter part of May? Approximately when?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't. I could not remember the exact date. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this is the same Ante Sliskovic to whom you gave an order to investigate Ahmici and who responded to you in a report dated the 25th of May, 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when he got this report concerning the Vitezovi, did you demand a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He informed me about this orally. I think, I think he also gave me a copy of this report, but he did make it clear to me that he sent the entire report to his superiors in Mostar, and about that I informed the chief of the main staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Sliskovic did, in fact, give you a copy of the report concerning the Vitezovi being involved; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I assume that he gave me a copy of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time this crime took place, the Vitezovi was attached to you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this problem of attachment was always there as far as the Vitezovi were concerned. It was selective. They interpreted it one way and I interpreted it another way. Attachment related to battle and it would be over as soon as that particular operation was over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question was whether you were attached -- whether he was attached, in your opinion, whether that person was attached, in your opinion. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were attached, but I never had legal authority over them in terms of punitive measures, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. For the time being, we can say that he was attached. Please continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you received this report concerning this war crime, did you give the report to the military district prosecutor so that he could file charges?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I probably put the report in the archives, and I informed the chief of the main staff about this. I did not directly cooperate with the prosecutor, but had I had the names of the suspects or the perpetrators, I certainly would have filed a criminal report with the military district prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, wasn't that your obligation as the commanding officer, to ensure that the military district prosecutor had as much information in your possession about this horrific crime?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that it was not specified individually who was the suspect and who was the perpetrator. Had I had that, I certainly would have provided the names to the district military prosecutor, but there wasn't anything like that in the report, except that the Vitezovi was behind this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got this report from Sliskovic and you saw that it didn't have names, did you demand names from Sliskovic, just like you wanted names on the Ahmici investigation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I certainly did ask for the investigation to be extended and to be continued. I did not get any subsequent reports from him, but I did receive information from him that he sent his report to the security administration in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not my question, General. Listen to my question. My question is: When you got this report from Sliskovic and you saw that it didn't have names, did you demand names from Sliskovic, just like you wanted names on the Ahmici investigation? Did you demand the names or did you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've already said that I asked and that I expected to receive this, but I did not receive these names from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there names in any of the files? Did Sliskovic tell you that there were names that were sent to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He told me that the details concerning this were sent to Mostar, but it was not my impression that he sent the names. In my conviction, there were no names in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you send him back out, in your zeal to find out facts about this crime, to gather information concerning names of the Vitezovi who were involved?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I asked the commander of the Vitezovi for that too, that he insist on it personally and that he gather information about this and that he take measures, because he was in charge in terms of discipline, and I was not in charge in terms of discipline. I insisted on the names, that is to say, who was behind this; however, I did not receive such a report from the commander of the Vitezovi or from the security assistant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question concerning your dealings with Sliskovic: General, after you received the report from Sliskovic, did you send Sliskovic back out to investigate this horrific crime so you could have the names of those members of the Vitezovi who were involved? Did you do that; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He continued to do so, and I requested that the investigation be continued, but every investigation which never ended and did not turn up with names and surnames was supposed to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened, General? Did you continually ask for the names while you were chief of staff and until you went to Croatia in November of 1995? What did you do? Do you have any paper to show us as to what you did?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not receive the names behind the crime at any time, but I received information that the perpetrators were the members of the Vitezovi, so I got that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the Vitezovi were involved in the attack on Grbavica in September of 1993, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not the whole unit, but part of the unit, yes. They took part according to a list of chosen soldiers, and it was their duty to send me a list of all the participants in the operation before the operation had begun, that is to say, in the preparatory stage of the operation. There were between 15 to 20 members of the Vitezovi, a maximum of 20 who took part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noted for us, on page 19676, in your testimony concerning the Vitezovi to my learned friend,

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: "A We took parts of certain units taking into consideration that these would be soldiers whom we could control and would carry out the orders which they were given in full." Were the Vitezovi soldiers that you picked for the attack on Grbavica involved in the truck bomb attack in Stari Vitez on 18 April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot answer that, whether they took part or not, but I know that I demanded of the commanders to select soldiers and that the soldiers that took part in the Grbavica operation fulfilled the orders they had received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you told us that you personally selected these soldiers for the Grbavica attack because they'd follow orders, you don't know whether or not these same soldiers were involved in this horrific crime in Stari Vitez, do you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never received a list of participants, the people who took part in the crime in Stari Vitez, the names of the Vitezovi, but for the Grbavica operation, I did demand that each commander should write and sign a guarantee for the soldiers selected. So the commander commanding the Vitezovi had to have a list of 20 or 15 soldiers, whatever the number, and he had to sign his name guaranteeing that they would perform their military duties, and there is a whole elaborated report on the Grbavica operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, had you demanded the names of the perpetrators of this crime, you would have known whether or not the soldiers selected for the Grbavica attack in September had participated in this crime; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I asked, on several occasions, the commanders of the Vitezovi to conduct an investigation vis-à-vis his soldiers and everything related to the truck bomb and the crime committed, and for the Grbavica operation, I demanded that they be selected soldiers and that their commanders should guarantee their conduct and steps. Judging by their conduct, I judged that there were no soldiers of that kind in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I followed the operation that took part in September 1993; I followed the conduct. I saw what the soldiers were doing and what the commander was doing, and it was a purely military operation which was attended by the offices of UNPROFOR as well, and a Major by rank came to congratulate them for the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact is that you don't know one way or the other what Vitezovi soldiers were involved in the Grbavica attack who may have committed criminal acts in Stari Vitez; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told Darko Kraljevic, for him to take disciplinary measures against his soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only him, but I informed the chief of the main staff of the HVO about everything that had taken place. I sent out an extraordinary report to him, and I asked him to undertake measures, of course, because I was not in the power to do so, to issue disciplinary or any other measures vis-à-vis these units who were independent and set apart from the structure of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure that you demanded that Darko Kraljevic be disciplined as well, is that right, for this crime?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not demand that Darko Kraljevic be punished. I just sent a report as I received it from the assistant for security, and I sent an extraordinary report to the chief of the HVO main staff. In that report, it did not say that he was the perpetrator. It said that it was the Vitezovi unit, and that is the report I sent out to the chief of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, as the commander in chief of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, did you send any request or demand to your superiors that members of the Vitezovi be punished?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the commander in chief of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, did you send a demand or a request to your superiors that members of the Vitezovi be punished for this terrible crime?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I sent the information which I had about the crime, and I know that the assistant for security sent the administration for security information about that crime which he had gathered. I could not ask individual punishment because I did not have the names of the perpetrators of that crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have one piece of paper -- one piece of paper -- that will demonstrate that you, in fact, sent this information to the main staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not have many papers which would show a lot of things. I have no single operative report. The only paper I have is the one I received from you on the 24th of April, the report or my report to the chief of the main staff. But there were many, many such reports, at least three a day and sometimes more, but I haven't got them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to be accurate, Mr. President, the report that the witness is talking about on the 24th of April came from the HVO. The HVO gave it to us, and then we gave it to the Defence just to make the record accurate. It is 6.00, Mr. President. I'm about to go on to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. That's where we will leave things for this evening. Tomorrow, we will resume at 10.00; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court stands adjourned.
